clinicalPearls: Hypophosphataemic rickets is a group of disorders in which chronic hypophosphataemia from renal phosphate wasting impairs growth-plate and bone mineralisation, causing rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

Most forms are FGF23-mediated: X-linked (PHEX, the commonest), autosomal dominant (FGF23) and autosomal recessive (DMP1, ENPP1); the main non-FGF23 form is hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH, SLC34A3).

The hallmark biochemistry is low serum phosphate, normal calcium, normal or low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and raised alkaline phosphatase, with PTH normal or only mildly raised, contrasting with the high PTH of calcipenic rickets.
Children show leg bowing, genu varum or valgum, short stature, delayed walking, a rachitic rosary, craniotabes and dental abscesses, without hypocalcaemic features.
The key distinction from nutritional rickets is normal calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D with hypophosphataemia and phosphaturia, and a lack of response to standard vitamin D ('vitamin D-resistant').
HHRH is set apart by appropriately raised 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and hypercalciuria and responds to phosphate alone, since active vitamin D can worsen hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis.
FGF23-mediated forms are treated with oral phosphate plus active vitamin D, or increasingly with burosumab for the X-linked type.
Early diagnosis and sustained treatment optimise linear growth and reduce deformity, though orthopaedic correction may be needed for residual bowing.
reference.pathophysiology: Normal mineralisation of the growth plate and osteoid depends on an adequate phosphate supply. In these disorders renal phosphate wasting produces chronic hypophosphataemia and defective mineralisation. In the FGF23-mediated forms, excess or overactive FGF23 downregulates proximal tubular sodium-phosphate cotransporters and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so calcitriol fails to rise appropriately. In HHRH, a defect in the NaPi-IIc cotransporter (SLC34A3) causes primary phosphate wasting with a compensatory, appropriate rise in calcitriol, driving intestinal calcium absorption, hypercalciuria and suppressed PTH. The final common consequence is accumulation of unmineralised osteoid at the growth plate (rickets) and in mature bone (osteomalacia).
additionalDifferentials: Fanconi syndrome and renal tubular acidosis
chronic kidney disease with renal osteodystrophy
additionalInvestigations: serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and PTH
urinary phosphate with tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TmP/GFR)
urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio to identify HHRH
wrist and knee radiographs for cupping, fraying and widened physes
genetic panel (PHEX, FGF23, DMP1, ENPP1, SLC34A3) and renal ultrasound
redFlags: failure to thrive or severe growth failure
reference.prognosis: With early and sustained treatment growth and deformity improve, but some residual short stature and orthopaedic problems commonly persist into adulthood.
pitfalls: labelling as nutritional rickets and treating with plain vitamin D alone
missing hypercalciuria in HHRH and worsening it with calcitriol
overlooking acquired causes such as tumour-induced osteomalacia in older children and adults
not measuring urinary phosphate to confirm renal wasting
references: Oxford Textbook of Endocrinology and Diabetes
management: Treat FGF23-mediated forms conventionally with oral phosphate supplements combined with an active vitamin D analogue such as calcitriol or alfacalcidol
Use the anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody burosumab as targeted therapy for X-linked hypophosphataemia where conventional treatment is inadequate
Treat hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria using phosphate supplementation alone, avoiding active vitamin D which worsens the hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis
Provide orthopaedic management of leg bowing and deformity, including corrective osteotomy where needed
Maintain dental surveillance and treat the characteristic dental abscesses
Monitor phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, renal function and urinary calcium, screening for nephrocalcinosis and treatment-induced hyperparathyroidism
Refer to paediatric endocrinology and offer genetic counselling appropriate to the specific inheritance, whether X-linked, autosomal dominant or recessive
